title: Fit nail plates where a bored hole is too close to the stud face
instruction: A cable runs through holes bored in the five studs. Fit a steel nail plate flat on the top face of each stud whose hole edge is less than 1-1/4 in (31.75 mm) below that face, centred over the hole, and plate no other stud. Then let go of the plates.
context: A drywall screw driven through a live NM cable can shock the installer or start a fire inside a finished wall. So the electrical code (NEC 300.4(A)(1)) requires a bored hole's edge to be at least 1-1/4 in (31.75 mm) from the nearest face of a stud; where it is closer, a steel nail plate at least 1/16 in thick goes over the hole before the drywall. A 22 mm hole in an 89 mm stud passes on both faces only if its top edge is 31.75 to 35.25 mm below the face, within about 1.75 mm of centre, so the call is read from the stud's side, as an electrician does. The wall here is a panel on a framing table, as in an off-site panel plant where rough-in is done on flat panels (on site it happens after the walls stand). The robot must judge each hole, plate only the studs that need it, and set each thin plate flat and centred on a 38 mm face. Done by: electricians, panel-plant assemblers, building inspectors.
setup: Positions in mm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y left, z up from the table top. Studs: five fixed pine 2x4s, 38 wide (y) x 89 deep (z) x 280 long (x), lying on edge with a 38 mm face up, from x 160 to 440, centred at y -240, -120, 0, 120 and 240. Each has a 22 mm hole bored across it (along y) centred at x 270, drawn on both side faces as a near-black 22 mm square. Hole centres lie 33, 36, 44.5, 28 and 45 mm below the up face (y -240 to 240), so their top edges are 22, 25, 33.5, 17 and 34 mm below it; every bottom edge is at least 33 mm above the down face, and every edge at least 16 mm (5/8 in) from both faces, as framing rules require. Cable: fixed yellow NM cable, 11 x 6 mm, through the hole centres, stepping between hole heights midway between studs, out to y -300 and 300. Plate stands: four fixed dark grey steel blocks, 20 (y) x 60 (x) x 40 mm tall, at x 100, y -150, -50, 50 and 150. Plates: four loose galvanized steel nail plates, 76 (x) x 38 (y) x 1.6 mm, 36 g, one lying flat on each stand, long side along x. Run with object jitter off: the plates sit on narrow stands. The setup screenshot's bottom strip shows two right-wrist camera frames over the studs at y -120 and y 0 (a check that the hole depths can be read), not the start pose.
scoring: Judged from the final state (a top photo and a ruler). A plate protects a stud when it lies flat on the stud's up face (its underside within 1 mm of the face, tilted under 5 degrees) with its long side along the stud (within 10 degrees), its centre within 3 mm of the stud's centreline (so it spans the 38 mm face) and within 20 mm of the hole's centre along the stud (so it covers the hole's length); it is still (under 1 cm/s); and no point on a gripper's centre line, from its wrist mount to its finger tips, is within 5 cm of any point of it. The studs that need a plate are those whose hole edge is under 31.75 mm from the face (y -240, -120 and 120). Score: 0.25 per protected stud, minus 0.25 per plate resting on the face of a stud that doesn't need one (y 0 or 240: its centre over the face, its underside within 5 mm of it, turned any way), never below 0, because a plate is a limited part and one on the wrong stud leaves a needed stud bare. A plate stacked, off the studs, left on its stand or on the floor earns nothing. 1.0 once every stud that needs a plate is protected with no plate on a wrong stud and this has held for 1 s; until then at most 0.75. The studs, cable and stands are fixed to the bench.
reset_notes: Lay the four plates back flat on their stands, long side along x. Run with object jitter 0 (with jitter the plates fall off their stands).
fidelity: Scaled bench mock-up: studs 280 mm long, 120 mm apart (406 mm on site). Rigid boxes: studs, cable and stands are fixed; each hole is a dark 22 mm square around the cable, not cut through. Plates are rigid 1.6 mm steel resting by friction (static 1.2, dynamic 1.0; real ones are nailed). Plates are staged on narrow stands so a parallel gripper can close under their edges; picking from a flat surface or a box is not tested. Scoring is geometric; grippers come from joint positions.
